# Managing Cardiovascular Risk in Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential

**Authors:** Ohad Oren; Aeron M. Small; Amy E. Lin; Peter Libby

**Affiliations:** aCardiology Division, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | bCardiovascular Division, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | cDivision of Cardiology, Section of Cardio-Oncology and Immunology, University of California-San Francisco, San Francisco, California, USA

TET2 and JAK2 CHIP are causally associated with accelerated atherosclerosis.

CHIP mutation and clone size guide cardioprotective intensity.

Ongoing clinical trials are evaluating targeted therapies for CHIP.

Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) is a preleukemic state in which a hematopoietic stem cell acquires a single leukemia driver mutation, resulting in clonal expansion.1 CHIP may be detected during the evaluation of unexplained blood count abnormalities or through germline testing in relatives of individuals with cancer. Furthermore, as cancer-directed therapies can induce genotoxic effects and promote clonal selection, people with or who have had cancer may manifest CHIP. Although CHIP confers an increased incidence of hematologic malignancies, most of the excess mortality results from cardiovascular disease.2,3

This primer reviews our approach to the cardiovascular assessment and care of individuals with CHIP using a clinical case.

## Clinical Case

A 59-year-old man with essential hypertension, diet-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, deep venous thrombosis, and localized melanoma was referred to the CHIP clinic because of a finding of BRAF, PLCG2, and TET2 CHIP during work-up for asymptomatic blood count abnormalities. Three months before referral, the patient had mild thrombocytosis (platelet count 501 × 109/L). His hemogram otherwise showed a hemoglobin concentration of 14.0 g/dL and a leukocyte count of 9 × 103/μL. Next-generation sequencing (NEBNext kit, New England Biolabs) detected pathogenic mutations involving TET2 (c.3581C>G) (variant allele fraction [VAF] 5.6%), BRAF (p.L597R) (VAF 4.1%), and PLCG2 (p.A708T) (VAF 2.8%).

The patient had localized melanoma of the shoulder 11 years prior requiring surgical excision. He led an active lifestyle and was a lifelong nonsmoker. He reported consuming 5 alcoholic drinks per week. His family history was notable for myocardial infarction in a paternal grandfather (in his 60s). His medications included aspirin 81 mg/d, atorvastatin 40 mg/d, lisinopril 2.5 mg/d, and apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily. Physical examination showed a heart rate of 68 beats/min, blood pressure of 112/74 mm Hg, weight of 98.1 kg, and a body mass index of 30.2 kg/m2. Twelve-lead electrocardiography demonstrated sinus rhythm. Laboratory work-up revealed a total cholesterol concentration of 139 mg/dL, a low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) concentration of 88 mg/dL, a high-density lipoprotein cholesterol concentration of 29 mg/dL, a triglyceride concentration of 111 mg/dL, and glycated hemoglobin of 6.1%.

## The Biological and Clinical Cardiovascular Implications of CHIP

With age, hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells acquire somatic mutations. The vast majority of these are silent, but those in a handful of known leukemia driver genes promote expansion of the mutant clone. If a clone acquires additional mutations (usually ≥2 more), progression to hematologic malignancy may ensue. An arbitrary cutpoint defines CHIP as the presence of a somatic mutation in a leukemia driver gene involving at least 2% of peripheral leukocytes in the absence of overt hematological disease, cytopenia, or morphologic dysplasia. Of note, CHIP represents one subgroup among the broader spectrum of clonal hematopoiesis, which also encompasses other forms of somatic mosaicism characterized by structural chromosomal alterations rather than the presence of a leukemia driver mutation.

CHIP rarely affects individuals younger than 40 years and occurs in as many as 11.7% among those 80 to 89 years of age.1 CHIP may occur “de novo” or following cytotoxic anticancer therapies. The most commonly mutated driver genes in “de novo” cases, including in patients with cancer, are DNMT3A, TET2, and ASXL1, which encode epigenetic regulators with roles in hypo- and hypermethylation.1 In contrast, therapy-related CHIP associates more commonly with recurrent mutations in TP53, PPM1D, and ATM, genes with key functions in DNA damage and repair response (DDR). Whether germline factors predispose to CHIP has not been elucidated, although DDR and telomere maintenance genes may play a role. Although CHIP is associated with an increased risk for hematologic malignancy, the absolute risk (annual incidence ∼ 0.5%-1%) does not account for the elevated mortality rates. Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) predominates as a contributor to that gap, with relative risks for coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction between 2 and 4 for CHIP carriers compared with those without CHIP, independent of conventional cardiovascular risk factors.1,2

Several investigations have established a causal link between certain forms of CHIP and inflammasome-driven atherosclerosis. In mice, bone marrow reconstitution with TET2-deficient cells increases atherosclerotic plaque size, an effect mediated by NLPR3 inflammasome activation and downstream increases in interleukin (IL)–1β and IL-6 expression.2,4 Additional evidence for the association among TET2 CHIP, inflammation, and coronary artery disease comes from an exploratory analysis of CANTOS (Canakinumab Antiinflammatory Thrombosis Outcome Study), in which patients with TET2 CHIP had reduced major adverse cardiovascular event rates when treated with a monoclonal antibody neutralizing IL-1β. In murine models of Jak2 V617F CHIP, activation of the AIM2 inflammasome contributed to development of atherosclerotic lesions and neutrophil extracellular traps, implicated in venous thrombosis.5 A UK Biobank analysis revealed strong associations between the presence of JAK2 mutations and both prevalent and incident venous thromboembolic risk.6 In experimental studies of aberrant DDR genes recapitulating TP53 and PPM1D CHIP, macrophage proliferation was increased in arterial plaques with consequent expansion in peripheral artery plaque.7

## How Do We Integrate CHIP Data Into Cardiovascular Risk Assessment?

Studies have demonstrated an independent association between CHIP and a higher incidence of ischemic cardiovascular events, with significant effect sizes in TET2 and JAK2 CHIP, especially with large (VAF > 10%) clones (Figure 1).1,2 Mechanistically, NLRP3 and AIM2 inflammasomes have been implicated in atherogenesis and thrombogenesis in Tet2 and Jak2 CHIP, respectively. Analyses have demonstrated that TET2 CHIP and JAK2 CHIP are associated with approximately 2- and 12-fold increases in ischemic cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction and stroke,2 conferring excess cardiovascular risk that resembles the magnitude of traditional cardiovascular risk factors.8 In addition, CHIP, in particular TET2 and PPM1D CHIP, independently potentiate the risk for ASCVD and mortality in patients who have had ischemic cardiac or cerebrovascular events. ## How Do We Approach Cardiovascular Prevention in Individuals With CHIP?

Given the current dearth of clinical trial evidence regarding management of CHIP, we can offer only our informed opinions at present. We do not screen for CHIP in unselected patients with cardiovascular disease, and many of our patients derive from our hematology and medical oncology colleagues following the detection of CHIP. Our CHIP clinic educates individuals and families about the nature of CHIP and the increased risk for ischemic cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events in particular subgroups, while acknowledging the evolving understanding of the associations.9 We provide a “patient page” of information for patients, their family members, and primary care physicians who may not have previously encountered CHIP.9 We stress the importance of maintaining healthy lifestyle habits in all patients, encouraging physical activity, the consumption of a healthy diet, and avoidance of smoking, vaping, and other nicotine products. In the absence of clinical trial evidence, we practice aggressive preventive cardiology and consider TET2, JAK2, PPM1D, and TP53 CHIP as secondary prevention equivalents and target lipid (LDL-C < 70 mg/dL), blood pressure (<130/80 mm Hg), and glycemic (glycated hemoglobin <6.5%) control (Figure 2). In individuals with large (VAF > 10%) TET2 or JAK2 CHIP, multiple TET2 CHIP, concomitant large TET2 and JAK2 mutations, or TET2 CHIP with elevated lipoprotein(a), which we consider particularly high risk, we strictly control lipids (LDL-C < 55 mg/dL) and blood pressure (<120/80 mm Hg).Figure 2Our Approach to Primary Prevention in Individuals With CHIPWe incorporate data on somatic mutation and clone size to devise a cardioprotective strategy. A1C = glycated hemoglobin; BP = blood pressure; CAD = coronary artery disease; CAS = carotid artery stenosis; DASH = Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension; LDL-C = low-density lipoprotein cholesterol; Lp(s) = lipoprotein(s); PAD = peripheral artery disease.gr2.jpg372332785729e47e01ba18f71975de566bf0f6LOAD_COMPLETED25042740715782urn:cdn:blobs/e290/12441604/785729e47e01/gr2.jpggr2.gif753245f9bb4aa4395d7b3ccf4b37509527cbdNEVER_LOAD9099urn:cdn:blobs/e290/12441604/5f9bb4aa4395/gr2.gif

In individuals with JAK2 CHIP, we also engage in shared decision making regarding the utility and risks of primary prevention with low-dose aspirin, for which we have a low threshold in people at low bleeding risk who have coronary artery disease, history of venous thromboembolism, or strong family history of ASCVD. In patients with TET2 or JAK2 CHIP with history of ASCVD, we intensify secondary prevention efforts, attempting to achieve the lowest reasonable LDL-C level, often using multiple lipid-lowering agents, including statins, ezetimibe, and proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitors, and we discuss with patients the addition of inclisiran or bempedoic acid on an individual basis. In persons with TET2 CHIP, we discuss empirical supplementation with vitamin C, a cofactor for the enzyme TET2, given preliminary evidence that it ameliorates DNA demethylation secondary to TET2 loss of function, although the optimal form and dose of vitamin C are unknown.10 In individuals with mutations in DDR genes, such as PPM1D and TP53, we pay special attention to arterial bruits, pedal pulses, and ankle-brachial index on examination, especially in those with concomitant risk factors for atherosclerosis, but we do not currently treat with empiric aspirin and/or rivaroxaban given their clinical equipoise in individuals with asymptomatic and stable peripheral arterial disease. Although individuals with CHIP have higher coronary artery calcium scores than those without CHIP, in asymptomatic patients we do not routinely screen for subclinical disease or perform ischemia testing unless clinically indicated, although we are more aggressive with lipid and blood pressure targets in individuals with TET2 or JAK2 CHIP and concomitant radiographic atherosclerotic disease (“particularly high risk” in Figure 2). We screen all patients with CHIP for arrhythmia and heart failure through a comprehensive history and physical examination, and we do not routinely advise laboratory or imaging testing in the absence of corresponding signs or symptoms.

We consider individuals with non-TET2, non-JAK2, and non-TP53/PPM1D CHIP, including DNMT3A CHIP, to have cardiovascular risk that is not clearly elevated beyond that of the general population on the basis of current evidence.

## Case Continued

We recommended the addition of ezetimibe 10 mg/d to achieve LDL-C <70 mg/dL. In the setting of hypertension, prior deep venous thrombosis, and TET2 CHIP, we advised the patient to continue low-dose daily aspirin. We also discussed vitamin C supplementation.

## Conclusions

In the coming decades, cardiovascular clinicians will be challenged with ameliorating the cardiovascular disease burden attributable to CHIP as the population continues to age and sequencing becomes more commonplace. Ongoing clinical trials—investigating an NLRP3 inflammasome inhibitor in patients with coronary artery disease and TET2 CHIP (GC43343) and a bispecific IL-1β and IL-18 inhibitor in patients with coronary artery disease and TET2 or DNMT3A CHIP (NCT06097663)—represent an exciting opportunity. However, outcome trials and U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval of CHIP-directed pharmacotherapies will not be immediate. In addition, although genome-editing technologies hold great promise for the design of CHIP therapeutics, multiple technological obstacles, including difficulties with tissue delivery and off-target effects, require consideration. In the meantime, we use existing science to inform risk stratification and use the available armamentarium of cardioprotection. Fundamentally, we practice intensive preventive cardiology pending clinical trial evidence regarding targeted therapies.
